nodes.name: Visual parity

nodes.title: Worktree and simulator cleanup

nodes.name: principle-attack-the-premise
nodes.title: Attack the Premise
nodes.description: Apply when two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Take a census of which actors hold the imbalance before the next fix, then question the premise instead of writing another fix that assumes it.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate

nodes.name: principle-boundary-discipline
nodes.title: Boundary Discipline
nodes.description: Apply when wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Concentrate guards at system boundaries (CLI, config, network, external APIs); trust internal types and keep business logic in pure functions.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters

nodes.name: principle-build-the-lever
nodes.title: Build the Lever
nodes.description: Apply to any non-trivial work, not just bulk work: edits, migrations, analyses, checks. Build the tool that does it or proves it (codemod, script, generator, or a skill your subagents follow) instead of working by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply to any non-trivial work, not just bulk work: edits, migrations, analyses, checks

nodes.name: principle-encode-lessons-in-structure
nodes.title: Encode Lessons in Structure
nodes.description: Apply when you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time, or notice a recurring correction. Encode the rule as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time, or notice a recurring correction

nodes.name: principle-exhaust-the-design-space
nodes.title: Exhaust the Design Space
nodes.description: Apply when facing a novel UI interaction or architectural decision with no precedent in the codebase. Build 2-3 competing prototypes and compare side by side before committing.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when facing a novel UI interaction or architectural decision with no precedent in the codebase

nodes.name: principle-experience-first
nodes.title: Experience First
nodes.description: Apply when product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs come up. Choose user delight over implementation convenience; ship fewer polished features over more rough ones.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs come up

nodes.name: principle-explain-the-number
nodes.title: Explain the Number
nodes.description: Apply before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured: a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result. Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured: a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result

nodes.name: principle-fix-root-causes
nodes.title: Fix Root Causes
nodes.description: Apply when debugging. Trace each symptom to its root cause and fix it there; reproduce first, ask why until you reach it, resist nil-check guards that silence crashes.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when debugging

nodes.name: principle-foundational-thinking
nodes.title: Foundational Thinking
nodes.description: Apply before writing logic: choosing core types and data structures, sequencing scaffold-vs-feature work, asking what concurrent actors share. Get the data structures right so downstream code becomes obvious.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply before writing logic: choosing core types and data structures, sequencing scaffold-vs-feature work, asking what concurrent actors share

nodes.name: principle-guard-the-context-window
nodes.title: Guard the Context Window
nodes.description: Apply when context is filling up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents; keep summaries in the main thread, not raw payloads.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when context is filling up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning

nodes.name: principle-laziness-protocol
nodes.title: Laziness Protocol
nodes.description: Apply when refactoring, evaluating diff size, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias toward deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when refactoring, evaluating diff size, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading

nodes.name: principle-make-operations-idempotent
nodes.title: Make Operations Idempotent
nodes.description: Apply when designing commands, lifecycle steps, or processing loops that run amid crashes, restarts, and retries. Converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when designing commands, lifecycle steps, or processing loops that run amid crashes, restarts, and retries

nodes.name: principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis
nodes.title: Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs
nodes.description: Apply when introducing a new internal API while old callers still exist. Migrate callers and delete the old API in the same wave instead of preserving compatibility layers.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when introducing a new internal API while old callers still exist

nodes.name: principle-minimize-reader-load
nodes.title: Minimize Reader Load
nodes.description: Apply when reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers between question and answer, and hidden state in the reader's head; collapse one-caller wrappers and shrink mutable scope.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace

nodes.name: principle-model-the-domain
nodes.title: Model the Domain
nodes.description: Apply when writing stateful logic, or when code branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when writing stateful logic, or when code branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files

nodes.name: principle-never-block-on-the-human
nodes.title: Never Block on the Human
nodes.description: Apply when tempted to ask 'should I do X?' on reversible work.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when tempted to ask 'should I do X?' on reversible work

nodes.name: principle-outcome-oriented-execution
nodes.title: Outcome-Oriented Execution
nodes.description: Apply during planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture; don't preserve smooth intermediate states with throwaway compatibility code.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply during planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries

nodes.name: principle-prove-it-works
nodes.title: Prove It Works
nodes.description: Apply after completing a task, before declaring done. Verify against the real artifact (run the feature, read the actual value, inspect the diff), not a proxy, self-report, or 'it compiles.'
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply after completing a task, before declaring done

nodes.name: principle-redesign-from-first-principles
nodes.title: Redesign From First Principles
nodes.description: Apply when integrating a new requirement into an existing design.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when integrating a new requirement into an existing design

nodes.name: principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state
nodes.title: Separate Before Serializing Shared State
nodes.description: Apply when concurrent actors might write to the same file, branch, key, or state object. Eliminate the sharing first; serialize structurally only when one shared writer is a real invariant.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when concurrent actors might write to the same file, branch, key, or state object

nodes.name: principle-sequence-verifiable-units
nodes.title: Sequence work into verifiable units
nodes.description: Apply to multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and to how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a verifiable state, check each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself to a reviewer.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply to multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and to how you stack commits and PRs

nodes.name: principle-subtract-before-you-add
nodes.title: Subtract Before You Add
nodes.description: Apply when sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead code, redundant validators, and stub references first, then build on the simpler base.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite

nodes.name: principle-test-behavior-not-implementation
nodes.title: Test Behavior, Not Implementation
nodes.description: Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Call the code as its users do and assert the exact result they see. Rewrite or delete a test that would pass if every imported function returned undefined.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when you write, change, or keep a test

nodes.name: principle-type-system-discipline
nodes.title: Type System Discipline
nodes.description: Apply when designing types, reviewing a function signature, or writing code in any statically-typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand semantic primitives, parse external data at boundaries, refuse to lie to the compiler, exhaust variants, derive from authoritative schemas.
nodes.appliesWhen: Apply when designing types, reviewing a function signature, or writing code in any statically-typed language

nodes.name: design-red-flags.md

nodes.description: Screen every candidate before synthesis. A red flag is a reason to revise or reject the shape.

The working directory is a git worktree when available, otherwise a per-runner subdirectory under the sketch dir. What matters is independence between candidates.

nodes.name: patterns.md

nodes.name: epistemics.md
nodes.title: Epistemics
nodes.description: How to reason about confidence when evidence is historical, fragmentary, and sometimes contradictory, and how to tell the user without flattening it into false certainty. Code shows what it does, not *why it exists*. The why lives in commits, PRs, tickets, docs, and conversations, all incomplete, biased, and sometimes missing. Pretending otherwise produces confident-sounding guesses that mislead the user.

nodes.name: investigator-prompt.md
nodes.title: Investigator Prompt Template
nodes.description: Fill in the placeholders. Append the one category playbook `sources/<source>.md` for this investigator's evidence category (index: `source-playbook.md`). If the target code looks defensive (null checks, retry logic, timeout handling, rate limiting, feature flags, egress guards, OOM handlers), also append `sources/incident-postmortem.md` so the investigator runs incident-flavored queries inside its own source.

nodes.name: source-playbook.md
nodes.title: Source playbooks
nodes.description: The why skill spawns one investigator per available evidence category, each reading a single source-specific playbook below. The playbooks are concrete examples for common MCPs. Adapt them for a different MCP in the same category.

nodes.name: code-archaeology.md
nodes.title: Code Archaeology (git + in-repo)
nodes.description: - Commit history (messages, dates, authors, diffs) - PR descriptions, review comments, and discussion threads (via `gh`) - Inline code comments, TODOs, FIXMEs, deprecation notes - ADRs (architectural decision records) if the repo keeps them - Tests, whose names and assertions often encode the edge cases that motivated a change - Related files modified in the same commits (co-change signal) - CHANGELOG entries and release notes in the repo - Issue/ticket IDs in commit messages and PR bodies

nodes.name: databricks.md
nodes.title: Databricks Analytics & System Tables
nodes.description: Databricks is the product-analytics, data-pipeline, and warehouse-telemetry layer. It complements Datadog. Datadog is the *infra/runtime* view, Databricks is the *product/data* view (what users did, which experiments ran, how feature usage evolved, where a threshold constant came from).

nodes.name: datadog.md
nodes.title: Datadog Telemetry
nodes.description: Datadog holds the runtime record, what actually happened in production, as opposed to what was planned or discussed.

nodes.name: incident-postmortem.md
nodes.title: Incident & Postmortem Context
nodes.description: - **Linear**: look for tickets labeled `incident`, `sev-*`, `postmortem-action-item`, `reliability` - **Slack**: search `#sev-*` and `#incident-*` channels around the dates the target code was added - **Git**: commits with messages like "fix for incident", "add defensive check", "revert" followed by "re-apply with..." are strong signals

nodes.name: linear.md
nodes.title: Linear Tickets
nodes.description: - Issues describing features, bugs, and their motivation - Project docs attached to issues (often PRDs or specs) - Parent/sub-issue relationships (broader initiative → specific tickets) - Comments on issues (clarifications, scope changes, "why we're doing this" rationale) - Labels (e.g., `compliance`, `customer-request`, `perf`) that signal the type of motivation - Status updates that explain scope changes - Attachments and linked GitHub PRs

nodes.name: notion.md
nodes.title: Notion Docs
nodes.description: - PRDs (product requirement documents) - Technical specs and RFCs - Architectural decision records (ADRs) - Meeting notes from design reviews - Team pages with domain context - Postmortems from incidents - Runbooks that may explain defensive code - Strategy documents that set priorities

nodes.name: architect

nodes.name: arena
nodes.title: Arena
nodes.description: Spawn N parallel candidates at the same task, pick a base, graft the strongest parts of the losers into it. Use for /arena, 'arena this', 'throw it in the arena', or when one attempt at a non-trivial artifact would lock in the wrong shape.

nodes.name: automate-me

nodes.name: benchmark-checklist

nodes.name: blast-radius

nodes.description: Find what a change could break somewhere else before it ships, beyond the diff, and prove the one fact it's safe because of by running real code instead of writing it up. Use for 'blast radius of X', 'what could this break', or reviewing a small diff you don't trust.

nodes.name: bro

nodes.name: create-verification-skill

nodes.name: figure-it-out

nodes.name: how

nodes.name: interrogate

nodes.name: ketchup
